messages.author: edd4914c326b6d31
messages.subject: prior for intercept
parts:
I'm estimating a logistic model and treat the parameters mostly as
beta[i] ~ normal(0, sigma_beta[sdclass[i]]
Where the beta are grouped into bunches by sdclass.

The intercept is beta[1]; it doesn't seem reasonable to group it with
anything else, since the prior that it's around 0 is less plausible.
But if I do this sdclass[1] is being estimated with only one parameter.
It certainly can't be estimated well, but is this at all reasonable?

Wrinkle: I'm using the Matt trick; the real specification looks like (in
shorthand)
beta_raw[1] ~ uniform(-5, 5)
beta_raw[2..J] ~ normal(0, 1)
beta[i] <- beta_raw[i]*sigma_beta[sdclass[i]]
sigma_beta ~ cauchy(0, 5) // sigma beta has ~ 4 elements

Can anyone comment on the wisdom of this (I suspect it is not wise!) and
suggest a better alternative?

I'm using this all in a model that is having problems, though I suspect
the main source of the problem is elsewhere, perhaps the fact that there
are 2 levels of clustering. But this seems worth cleaning up.

Thanks.
Ross Boylan

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] prior for intercept
parts:
Why not just pull the intercept out of the beta term and
give it whatever prior you think is reasonable?

If there's some other reason to keep everything in the same
vector, you could write:

beta_raw[1] ~ ...whatever...
for (j in 2:J)
beta[j] <- beta_raw[j-1] * sigma_beta[sdclass[j-1]];

declaring sdclass and beta_raw to be of size J-1 rather than size J.

- Bob

On 12/7/13, 12:34 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> One thing is, it's completely kosher in Stan to just add another prior for beta[1] or sdclass[1] on top of everything else.
>
> On Dec 7, 2013, at 3:01 AM, Ross Boylan wrote:
>
>> I'm estimating a logistic model and treat the parameters mostly as
>> beta[i] ~ normal(0, sigma_beta[sdclass[i]]
>> Where the beta are grouped into bunches by sdclass.
>>
>> The intercept is beta[1]; it doesn't seem reasonable to group it with anything else, since the prior that it's around 0 is less plausible. But if I do this sdclass[1] is being estimated with only one parameter. It certainly can't be estimated well, but is this at all reasonable?
>>
>> Wrinkle: I'm using the Matt trick; the real specification looks like (in shorthand)
>> beta_raw[1] ~ uniform(-5, 5)
>> beta_raw[2..J] ~ normal(0, 1)
>> beta[i] <- beta_raw[i]*sigma_beta[sdclass[i]]
>> sigma_beta ~ cauchy(0, 5) // sigma beta has ~ 4 elements
>>
>> Can anyone comment on the wisdom of this (I suspect it is not wise!) and suggest a better alternative?

Your suspicion is right.

The primary problem with the above is that there's no way to define a
parameter beta_raw in Stan that has support (-5,5) in dimension 1 and (-inf,inf)
elsewhere.

It'd be easier to declare beta_raw to be of size J-1,
sdlcass to not include the intercept, and then take:

alpha ~ ...whatever prior you want for intercept...

beta_raw ~ normal(0,1);

Then there's one of two options. Closest to what you did
is put everything back together into a beta vector:

beta[1] <- alpha;
for (j in 2:J)
beta[j] <- beta_raw[j-1] * sigma_beta[sdclass[j-1]];

The alternative is to just use the intercept directly in the
regression. The second option seems clearer because it doesn't
have the ugly off-by-one indexing and makes the role of the separate
prior clearer.

Stan supports the (vector + scalar) operation, which
adds the scalar to each dimension of the vector. So you can
still use matrix arithmetic in the linear predictor part of
the regression.

- Bob

With some of the earlier models I fit I found that pre-specifying the

parameters.

Ross

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] prior for intercept
parts:
What I'm saying is that unless you constrain beta_raw in
its declaration, the model's ill formed.

Conventions vary. That's what R requires you to do, but
if you look at books, they use different conventions.

On 12/7/13, 5:00 PM, Ross Boylan wrote:
> On Sat, 2013-12-07 at 13:45 -0500, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>> Why not just pull the intercept out of the beta term and
>> give it whatever prior you think is reasonable?
>>
>> If there's some other reason to keep everything in the same
>> vector, you could write:
>>
>> beta_raw[1] ~ ...whatever...
>> for (j in 2:J)
>> beta[j] <- beta_raw[j-1] * sigma_beta[sdclass[j-1]];
>>
>> declaring sdclass and beta_raw to be of size J-1 rather than size J.
>>
> It seemed more like conventional notation to make beta[1] the intercept.

Conventions vary. Andrew and Jennifer's book compare several for
several different kinds of models.

> But I have already given it a special distribution, as I indicated for
> the "real" specification:
> beta_raw[1] ~ uniform(-5, 5)
> beta_raw[2..J] ~ normal(0, 1)
>
> Are you saying that rather than estimate sigma for beta[1] to just
> specify a prior and be done with it?
Yes.

> E.g., now I have
> beta_raw[1] ~ uniform(-5, 5)
> sigma_beta[1] ~ cauchy(0, 5)
> beta[1] <- beta_raw[1] * sigma_beta[1]
>
> whereas I could just have
> beta_raw[1] ~ uniform(-5, 5)
> beta[1] <- beta_raw[1] // if I keep my current handling of the
> intercept
>

IMPORTANT: For robustness, Stan models need to have non-zero probability
for all variables satisfying declared constraints (i.e., the type
declarations define the intended support). Any parameter values that satisfy
declared constraints but have 0 probability will get rejected, and if you init
there you'll never move and if the proper estimate is close, sampling will
be very inefficient.

So you can fix your model by constraining all beta_raw to fall
between -5 and 5, or by removing the uniform distribution on beta_raw
and giving it a prior with support on all of (-inf, inf).

> With some of the earlier models I fit I found that pre-specifying the
> scale parameter often worked poorly.

See Andrew's blog for discussion of informative priors. You should
set them based on what you know about their possible values from
what you're trying to model.

You can use whatever prior you want for beta_raw[1]. The compound
uniform-Cauchy is an unusual choice. You could just use a cauchy(0,5)
if you want something that will allow extreme values given enough data.
The tighter the prior, the more stable the computations will be.

> BTW I upped the target acceptance rate to 90% (after seeing the comments
> here and on dev that hierarchical models often need higher acceptance
> rates) and the estimates are behaving pretty well.

How does 0.8 work? That's going to be our new default based on some
theoretical work Michael's doing.

> sigma_beta[1] had a
> median of 1.2 but a mean of 2.1. beta[1] had mean and median of -1.4
> (sd = 0.8). sigma_beta[1] had a much lower n_eff than most of the
> parameters.

Nor surprising --- sigma_beta[1] is the latent parameter in the
compound prior you set up.

- Bob

messages.author: edd4914c326b6d31
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] prior for intercept
parts:
I got good results with an acceptance rate of 0.8 and some tweaks to the
priors. I just realized they were not exactly what I intended, and that
I still have conflicts between the declared support on the
distributions..

Over 3/4 of the parameters had effective sample sizes = number of
iterations. That seems a little too good to be true.

As for the changes, I omitted the estimation of a scale parameter for
the intercept. My effort to get the support of the prior to match the
corresponding declaration went too far.

declaration prior
old:
intercept N Y
other N N

new:
intercept Y Y
other Y N

"other" means non-intercept beta parameters.
N = no bounds
Y = bounded

The old problem was that the intercept had a bounded prior but an
unbounded declaration; the new problem is that the other terms have
unbounded priors but bounded declarations!

Doing this right would require either giving the intercept and other
beta different parameter names so that I can remove the bound on the
other parameters, or accepting the bounds throughout.

On the one hand, it would be outlandish if any effects were bigger than
5; on the other hand, putting a bound on a parameter that is then
multiplied by an arbitrary positive number seems silly.

I wonder if the bounds on all parameters contributed to the speed of the
solution (the iterations ran about 3x faster, even ignoring the increase
in n_eff).


Ross

Code for now (excerpts for beta):
parameters {
vector<lower=-5,upper=5>[J] beta_raw; // standard covariate coefficients
real<lower=0> sigma_beta[NSD];
}
transformed parameters {
vector[J] beta;
beta[1] <- beta_raw[1]; for(ir in 2:J) {
for(ir in 2:J) {
beta[ir] <- beta_raw[ir]*sigma_beta[SDClass[ir]];
}
}
model {
sigma_beta ~ cauchy(0, 5);
beta_raw[1] ~ uniform(-5, 5); // redundant give bounds
for (j in 2:J) {
beta_raw[j] ~ normal(0, 1); // inconsistent with bounds
}
....

NUTS is very effective if the posterior's normal.

The effective sample sizes are estimated as shown in the manual,
using a conservative variance estimate based on the same chain
splitting and within/across calculations as for R-hat.

Exactly --- that's what I was trying to say in my previous reply

> On the one hand, it would be outlandish if any effects were bigger than
> 5; on the other hand, putting a bound on a parameter that is then
> multiplied by an arbitrary positive number seems silly.

Not silly if you want to help identify it. Better yet to
skip the multiplication and just use the "arbitrary" positive number.
That's what I was suggesting for reparameterization by pulling
the intercept out from the slopes.

> I wonder if the bounds on all parameters contributed to the speed of the
> solution (the iterations ran about 3x faster, even ignoring the increase
> in n_eff).

Yes --- tightening priors will help --- it has the effect of tightening
the prior on the unconstrained space where sampling is done.
The chapter near the end of the manual provides details, but you'll need
to ask Michael for intuitions about the geometric aspects of the problem.

- Bob
